drivers.name: Allen & Heath Avantis Digital Mixer
drivers.author: OpenAVC
drivers.description: Controls Allen & Heath Avantis digital mixing consoles via MIDI over TCP/IP on port 51325. Every input, group, aux, matrix, FX send/return, main, DCA, mute group and UFX send/return is a child entity with live mute / fader / name / colour state — the console's own channel names become the labels in OpenAVC. Send levels, main / DCA / mute-group assigns, Scene Recall (1-500), MMC transport and UFX global key / scale, with bidirectional state from console-side moves and a Get-probe watchdog that flips the device offline if the console vanishes.

help.overview: Controls an Allen & Heath Avantis digital mixing console over the network using MIDI over TCP/IP. Every channel strip is listed as a child entity with live state — bind child state (e.g. device.<id>.input.in01.mute) to panel elements and drive mutes, faders and scene recall from macros and buttons. The console's channel names and colours are read on connect and become the labels shown in OpenAVC; console-side moves push straight back into state.
help.setup:
1. Confirm the console is running firmware V2.0 or later. TCP/IP control is unavailable on earlier firmware.
2. Connect the Avantis to the same network as the OpenAVC server.
3. On the Avantis, go to Utility / Network and note the IP address.
4. Go to Utility / Control / MIDI and note the base MIDI channel (default 12). The console reserves the next four channels above the base for output buses, so the base cannot exceed 12.
5. Enter the IP address and matching base MIDI channel in the device config. The default port (51325) is correct.
6. Save. The channels appear under the device with live state; channel names and colours sync from the console automatically.

compatible_models.notes: Same MIDI command surface across the Avantis family. Requires console firmware V2.0 or later for TCP/IP control.

drivers.name: Allen & Heath dLive Digital Mixer
drivers.author: OpenAVC
drivers.description: Controls Allen & Heath dLive digital mixing systems (MixRack + Surface) via MIDI over TCP/IP on port 51325. Every input, group, aux, matrix, FX send/return, main, DCA, mute group and UFX send/return is a child entity with live mute / fader / name / colour state, and all 128 preamp sockets are children with live gain / pad / 48V state — the console's own channel names become the labels in OpenAVC. Send levels and assigns, per-channel HPF, Scene Recall (MixRack, 1-500), Cue List Recall (Surface, 1-2000), MMC transport and UFX global key / scale, with bidirectional state from console-side moves and a Get-probe watchdog that flips the device offline if the console vanishes.

help.overview: Controls an Allen & Heath dLive digital mixing system over the network using MIDI over TCP/IP. Every channel strip and preamp socket is listed as a child entity with live state — bind child state (e.g. device.<id>.input.in001.mute) to panel elements and drive mutes, faders, preamps and scene recall from macros and buttons. The console's channel names and colours are read on connect and become the labels shown in OpenAVC; console-side moves push straight back into state.
help.setup:
1. Confirm the dLive system is running firmware V2.0 or later. TCP/IP control is unavailable on earlier firmware.
2. Connect the MixRack (or Surface, if controlling the Surface directly) to the same network as the OpenAVC server.
3. On the dLive, go to Utility / Network and note the IP address.
4. Go to Utility / Control / MIDI and note the base MIDI channel. The console reserves the next four channels above the base for output buses.
5. Enter the IP address and matching base MIDI channel in the device config. Use port 51325 for MixRack, 51328 for Surface.
6. Save. The channels and preamp sockets appear under the device with live state; channel names and colours sync from the console automatically.

compatible_models.notes: Same MIDI command surface across the dLive S- and C-class Surfaces and DM-series MixRacks. Requires firmware V2.0 or later for TCP/IP control. Plain-TCP only (port 51325 MixRack / 51328 Surface); the TLS+UserProfile ports (51327 / 51329) are a future extension.

drivers.name: Allen & Heath Qu Digital Mixer
drivers.author: OpenAVC
drivers.description: Controls the Allen & Heath Qu family (Qu-16, Qu-24, Qu-32, Qu-Pac, Qu-SB) via MIDI over TCP/IP on port 51325. Auto-identifies the model on connect and registers every input, stereo input, mix, group, matrix, DCA, mute group and FX send/return as a child entity with live mute / fader / pan state and its real channel name. Mute / fader / pan / send / assign / pre-post control, DCA and mute-group masters, PAFL, local preamp gain and 48V, scene recall (1-100), MMC transport, channel naming and remote shutdown, with bidirectional state from console-side moves.

help.overview: Controls an Allen & Heath Qu mixer over MIDI-over-TCP. On connect the driver asks the console to identify itself, learns the model and MIDI channel, and lists every channel as a child entity with live mute / fader / pan state and its real name. Bind child state (e.g. device.<id>.input.in05.mute) to panel elements, and drive Set Fader / Mute / Recall Scene from macros and buttons. Console-side moves push straight back into state.
help.setup:
1. Connect the Qu to the same network as the OpenAVC server.
2. On the Qu, go to Setup / Network and note the IP address.
3. Enter the IP address above. Port 51325 is correct and the model/MIDI channel are detected automatically.
4. Save. Within a second or two the device connects, the model populates, and each channel appears under the device with its live state and name.

Notes:
  * The Qu allows only ONE TCP MIDI connection at a time — close Qu-Pad / other MIDI clients before connecting.
  * If the model doesn't populate, set it manually in the config as a fallback and run the Re-identify action.
  * The Qu drops idle MIDI connections; the driver keeps the link alive automatically.

compatible_models.notes: Verified end-to-end against a real Qu-16 (firmware V1.97): All-Call identify + full-state sync, child-entity registration with live channel names, and mute / fader / pan write round-trips confirmed by re-reading board state.

Same MIDI protocol and command surface as the Qu-16; the console reports its model over the All-Call SysEx, so the driver registers the right channel set automatically. Not yet tested on this hardware. Qu allows only one TCP MIDI connection at a time. The newer Qu-5/6/7 consoles use a different protocol and are not covered.

drivers.name: Allen & Heath SQ Digital Mixer
drivers.author: OpenAVC
drivers.description: Controls Allen & Heath SQ-5, SQ-6 and SQ-7 digital mixing consoles via MIDI over TCP/IP on port 51325. Every input, group, aux, matrix, FX send/return, DCA and mute group is a child entity with live mute / level / pan state and a channel picker on its commands. Scene recall (1-300), 1 dB nudges, SoftKey triggers, master balances, and bidirectional state — console-side moves push back into OpenAVC, and a Get-probe watchdog flips the device offline if the console vanishes.

help.overview: Controls an Allen & Heath SQ digital mixing console over the network using MIDI over TCP/IP. Every channel strip is listed as a child entity with live mute, level and pan state — bind child state (e.g. device.<id>.input.in05.mute) to panel elements and drive mutes, faders and scene recall from macros and buttons. Console-side moves push straight back into OpenAVC state.
help.setup:
1. Connect the SQ to the same network as the OpenAVC server.
2. On the SQ, go to Utility → General → Network and note the IP address.
3. Go to Utility → General → MIDI and note the MIDI Channel.
4. Enter the IP address and matching MIDI channel in the device config. The default port (51325) is correct.
5. Save. The channels appear under the device with live state; rename them in the project as needed (the SQ MIDI protocol does not expose console channel names).

compatible_models.notes: Same MIDI command set and channel counts across all three. SQ-5 has 8 SoftKeys (triggers 9-16 are no-ops). SoftKeys are addressed by integer 1-16.

drivers.name: AtlasIED Atmosphere
drivers.author: OpenAVC
drivers.description: Controls AtlasIED Atmosphere AZM4 and AZM8 audio processing and control systems over the third-party JSON-RPC protocol on TCP port 5321. Models sources, zones, mixes, groups, messages, routines, scenes, GPO presets, GPOs, and bell schedules as child entities labelled with the names from the Atmosphere configuration. Covers gain and mute per source / zone / mix / group, zone and group source select, group combine, message / routine / scene / GPO-preset triggers, GPO pin state, and today's bell schedule. Subscribes for state updates on connect.

help.overview:
AtlasIED Atmosphere is a configurable audio DSP / mixer / paging system widely deployed in restaurants, retail, fitness, and house-of-worship installs. This driver speaks the third-party JSON-RPC protocol on TCP port 5321. It subscribes to entity state on connect, so updates push live as users change settings on the front panel or in the web UI.

Sources, zones, mixes, groups, messages, routines, scenes, GPO presets, GPOs, and bell schedules appear as child entities, labelled with the names assigned during device configuration (via the Atmosphere web UI). Indices are zero-based, matching the device's Settings → Third Party Control → Message Table.

Entity names and GPO pin states are read-only over third-party control — rename entities in the Atmosphere web UI, and drive GPOs by recalling GPO presets.
help.setup:
1. In the Atmosphere web UI, go to Settings → Third Party Control → General and toggle 'Enable' on for the third-party control API.
2. Confirm the Atmosphere has a static IP (or DHCP reservation).
3. In OpenAVC, enter the IP. Port 5321 is fixed.
4. Set the entity counts (zones, sources, mixes, groups) to match the device configuration. Counts default to AZM8 sizing; over-sizing is harmless but bigger than needed clutters the child entity lists.
5. After connecting, confirm the source / zone / mix / group names from the Atmosphere config show up as the child entity labels.

compatible_models.notes: AZM4 / AZM8 are the standalone DSPs; AZMP4 / AZMP8 add internal amplification but share the same third-party control surface.

drivers.name: Dante DDM / Director
drivers.author: OpenAVC
drivers.description: Controls Dante audio routing via the Audinate Managed API. Requires Dante Domain Manager or Dante Director Professional. Each Dante device is a child entity; route/unroute any Rx channel to a Tx channel and monitor live subscription status.

help.overview:
This driver connects to a Dante Domain Manager (DDM) or Dante Director Professional instance to control audio routing across all Dante devices on the network. It does NOT connect to individual Dante devices — the DDM/Director acts as the central management point.

Every Dante device in the domain appears as a child entity. Each device's Rx channels show what they're currently subscribed to, so you can see and drive the whole routing matrix from one device.
help.setup:
1. You need Dante Domain Manager (on-premise) or Dante Director Professional (cloud) — the Standard tier does not include API access.
2. Generate an API key in the DDM/Director web UI.
3. Enter the DDM/Director URL (e.g., https://ddm.local or the Director cloud URL).
4. Enter the API key.
5. Enter the Dante domain name to manage (shown in DDM/Director).
6. On connect, the devices and channels are discovered. Use the 'Refresh from Device' button (or the 'refresh' command) after adding gear to the domain.

drivers.name: Audio-Technica ATDM-0604
drivers.author: OpenAVC
drivers.description: Controls Audio-Technica ATDM-0604 Digital SmartMixer via TCP with real-time multicast push updates. Inputs and outputs are child entities with fader, gain, mute, and live meters, labelled by the mixer's own channel names. Preset recall, SmartMix and AEC configuration, USB output routing, and AT-LINK mode.

help.overview: Controls Audio-Technica ATDM-0604 Digital SmartMixer. The ATDM-0604 is a 6-input automatic mixer designed for conference and installed sound applications.
help.setup:
1. Connect the ATDM-0604 to the network (default control port 17300). 2. Configure the mixer's IP address via the front panel or Web Remote. 3. To let OpenAVC find the mixer in a network scan, enable
   "Allow Discovery" (UPnP) in the mixer's network settings.
4. Input channels: 1-6 (mic/line) and ST (stereo).
   Output channels: 1-2 and ST (stereo).
5. Front-panel and Web Remote changes appear in OpenAVC instantly:
   the mixer multicasts change notices (factory default group
   225.0.0.100, port 17000) and OpenAVC listens automatically. If you
   changed the multicast address or port in Web Remote's network
   settings, set the matching values in this device's Notification
   Group / Notification Port fields. The mixer and the OpenAVC server
   must be on the same VLAN, and switches with IGMP snooping need an
   IGMP querier — if notices are filtered, control still works and
   changes appear at the poll interval instead.
6. Enable Level Meters (off by default) streams live input/output
   meters into OpenAVC at about two updates per second — bind panel
   meter elements to the meter state values.

drivers.name: Audio-Technica ATDM-0604a
drivers.author: OpenAVC
drivers.description: Controls Audio-Technica ATDM-0604a Digital SmartMixer via TCP with real-time multicast push updates. Inputs and outputs are child entities with fader, mute, preamp gain, source select, phantom power, and live meters, labelled by the mixer's own channel names. Preset recall, SmartMix and AEC configuration, USB output routing, test oscillator, and front-panel lockout.

help.overview: Controls the Audio-Technica ATDM-0604a Digital SmartMixer, a 6-input automatic mixer for conference and installed sound applications. Each input and output appears as a child entity carrying its fader, mute, gain, and settings, labelled with the channel name configured on the mixer.
help.setup:
1. Connect the ATDM-0604a to the network (default control port 17300). 2. Configure the mixer's IP address via Web Remote (http://<mixer-ip>/). 3. To let OpenAVC find the mixer in a network scan, enable
   "Allow Discovery" (UPnP) in the mixer's network settings.
4. Inputs 1-6 and Input ST, Outputs 1-2 and Output ST appear as this
   device's child entities, labelled by the channel names set on the
   mixer (rename them with the Rename commands or in Web Remote).
5. Front-panel and Web Remote changes appear in OpenAVC instantly:
   the mixer multicasts change notices (factory default group
   239.0.0.100, port 17000) and OpenAVC listens automatically. If you
   changed the multicast address or port in Web Remote's network
   settings, set the matching values in this device's Notification
   Group / Notification Port fields. The mixer and the OpenAVC server
   must be on the same VLAN, and switches with IGMP snooping need an
   IGMP querier — if notices are filtered, control still works and
   changes appear at the poll interval instead. Channel names and
   input settings have no change notice and refresh at the poll
   interval.
6. Enable Level Meters (off by default) streams live input/output
   meters into OpenAVC at about two updates per second — bind panel
   meter elements to the child meter values.

drivers.name: Audio-Technica ATDM-1012
drivers.author: OpenAVC
drivers.description: Controls Audio-Technica ATDM-1012 and ATDM-1012DAN Digital SmartMixers via TCP with real-time multicast push updates. Inputs, sub-inputs, outputs, and SmartMix groups are child entities with fader, mute, gain, source select, bus routing, and live meters, labelled by the mixer's own channel names. Preset recall, operator faders, USB output routing, test oscillator, and front-panel lockout.

help.overview: Controls Audio-Technica ATDM-1012 / ATDM-1012DAN Digital SmartMixers. The ATDM-1012 is a 10-input, 8-output automatic mixer with 12 mix buses, designed for conference rooms, courtrooms, and council chambers. The DAN variant adds Dante audio networking. Each input, sub-input, output, and SmartMix group appears as a child entity, labelled with the channel name configured on the mixer.
help.setup:
1. Connect the ATDM-1012 to the network (default control port 17300). 2. Configure the mixer's IP address via the front panel or Web Remote. 3. To let OpenAVC find the mixer in a network scan, enable
   "Allow Discovery" (UPnP) in the mixer's network settings.
4. Inputs 1-10, ST1/ST2, Sub-inputs 1-8, Outputs 1-8 and ST1/ST2, and
   SmartMix Groups 1-4 appear as this device's child entities, labelled
   by the names set on the mixer (rename them with the Rename commands
   or in Web Remote).
5. Front-panel and Web Remote changes appear in OpenAVC instantly:
   the mixer multicasts change notices (factory default group
   225.0.0.100, port 17000) and OpenAVC listens automatically. If you
   changed the multicast address or port in Web Remote's network
   settings, set the matching values in this device's Notification
   Group / Notification Port fields. The mixer and the OpenAVC server
   must be on the same VLAN, and switches with IGMP snooping need an
   IGMP querier — if notices are filtered, control still works and
   changes appear at the poll interval instead. Channel names and
   input settings have no change notice and refresh at the poll
   interval.
6. Enable Level Meters (off by default) streams live input/output
   meters into OpenAVC at about two updates per second — bind panel
   meter elements to the child meter values.
7. The ATDM-1012DAN uses the same protocol with added Dante settings.

drivers.name: Behringer X32 Digital Mixer
drivers.author: OpenAVC
drivers.description: Controls Behringer X32 and X32 Compact digital mixing consoles via OSC. 32 input channels, 8 aux ins, 8 FX returns, 16 mix buses, 6 matrices, 8 DCAs, and stereo/mono mains as child entities with fader, mute, and console-side names, plus scene recall and a liveness watchdog. Also compatible with Midas M32.

help.overview: Controls a Behringer X32 or X32 Compact digital mixer over the network using the OSC (Open Sound Control) protocol. Every strip is a child entity — all 32 input channels, 8 aux ins, 8 FX returns, 16 mix buses, 6 matrices, 8 DCAs, and the stereo/mono mains — with fader, mute, and the console's own scribble-strip name as the child label.
help.setup:
1. Connect the X32 to the same network as the OpenAVC server. 2. On the X32, go to Setup > Network and note the IP address. 3. Enter the IP address in the device config. The default port is 10023. 4. The driver will automatically subscribe to feedback and start
   receiving fader/mute updates. Strip names load on connect and
   become the child labels.

compatible_models.notes: Identical OSC protocol to X32.

drivers.name: Biamp Tesira TTP
drivers.author: OpenAVC
drivers.description: Controls Biamp Tesira and TesiraFORTÉ DSPs over the Tesira Text Protocol on TCP port 23 (Telnet). Supports Mute, Level, Source Selector, Matrix Mixer (crosspoints), Auto Mixer, Router, Logic, AEC, Room Combiner, Audio Meter, Signal Present Meter, Tone Generator, Preset recall, and basic VoIP / Dialer surfaces. Subscribes to push updates instead of polling. Declare your Tesira blocks once in the device config — each block becomes a child entity whose per-channel controls panel UIs bind to directly.

help.overview: Comprehensive Biamp Tesira / TesiraFORTÉ control over TTP (Telnet, port 23). The driver subscribes to per-block, per-channel state changes — UI bindings update in real-time without polling. Declare every Tesira block you want to monitor or control in the 'DSP Block List' table on the device page; each block becomes a child entity whose per-channel controls (levels, mutes, crosspoints, sources) panel elements bind to. Drive them with the Set / Toggle / Step Control commands: pick the block, then its control.
help.setup:
STEP 1 — Enable network control on the DSP.
Open Tesira software, connect to the unit, and go to Tools → Device Maintenance → Network Settings. Tick 'Discovery Service' and 'Telnet' (both default OFF). Leave 'System Security' OFF too — this driver expects an unauthenticated Telnet session, which matches the standard deployment when the DSP is on a private AV VLAN. Apply.

STEP 2 — Find your Instance Tags.
Open the Tesira design (.tmf file) for this DSP. Each control block (Mute, Level, Source Selector, Mixer, AEC, Room Combiner, etc.) has a user-assigned 'Instance Tag' — right-click any block → Properties → top of the dialog. Tags are case-sensitive: 'Level1' and 'level1' are NOT the same. For multi-channel blocks (e.g. a 4-mic Mute), note how many channels are wired up — that's the channel count you'll declare below.

STEP 3 — Enter the device IP address above.

STEP 4 — Declare your blocks in the 'DSP Block List' table on the device page.
Add a row per block: its Instance Tag, its Block Type (from the dropdown), and — for per-channel blocks or a matrix mixer — the Channels / NxM cell:
    • Channels can be '1', '1-4' (range), or '1,3,5' (list)
    • For a Matrix Mixer, use INPUTS x OUTPUTS (e.g. 8x4 = 8 inputs, 4 outputs)
    • Leave Channels blank and channel 1 is assumed
A new device starts with an example conferencing-room roster (mic mute/level, program level + mute, source select) — edit those rows to match your Tesira design, add rows for AEC / Room Combiner / Matrix Mixer as needed, and remove the ones you don't use.

STEP 5 — Save.
Within seconds the device should show 'Connected'. Each block you declared appears as a child entity — e.g. the 'Level1' block exposes a 'level_3' control for its third channel. Bind those child controls to UI elements, or drive them with the Set / Toggle / Step Control commands (pick the block, then its control) in macros and panel buttons.

Troubleshooting:
    • 'Connection lost' loop on port 22 — that's SSH, not       supported. Use port 23 (Telnet).
    • Device shows Connected but no state variables —       check that Telnet is enabled in System Manager AND       that your Instance Tags match exactly (case       matters).
    • Some channels don't update — verify the channel       count in your block list matches the actual wired       channel count in the Tesira design.
    • Need a block type the driver doesn't handle? Use       the generic 'Send Raw TTP Command' / 'Set       Attribute' commands — anything Tesira's command       string calculator generates will work.

compatible_models.notes: Every Tesira / TesiraFORTÉ DSP that runs Tesira software shares the same TTP protocol. Driver covers the block types AV integrators commonly use for room control. Setup: in Tesira's System Manager → Network Settings, enable Discovery and Telnet (both default OFF). Leave System Security disabled for the no-credentials path used by this driver.

drivers.name: SoundCoreHero Audio System
drivers.author: Wiktor Myszolow (Hero AV)
drivers.description: Controls a SoundCoreHero multi-zone audio distribution system (zones, players, speakers, inputs) over its HTTPS/WebSocket API.

help.overview: SoundCoreHero is a professional multi-zone audio distribution and management system. This driver exposes its zones, players, speakers and inputs as child entities, controls volume/mute/transport, and plays announcements.
help.setup:
1. Note the device IP. By default only HTTPS (port 443) is enabled.
2. Create or pick a user account in Settings -> Users. The driver logs in with that account's email and password to obtain a session (required by the control WebSocket).
3. Enter IP, email and password. Leave 'Verify SSL' off if the device uses its default self-signed certificate.

drivers.name: Onkyo / Integra / Pioneer AV Receiver (eISCP)
drivers.author: OpenAVC
drivers.description: Controls Onkyo, Integra, and Pioneer A/V receivers over the network using eISCP (the Integra Serial Control Protocol over Ethernet, TCP 60128). Power, mute, master volume, input selection, and listening-mode (DSP) selection, with polled power / mute / input / listening mode / volume status. The "!1" ISCP header, the CR terminator, and the 16-byte eISCP packet header with its computed data length are declared once and wrap every command.

help.overview: Onkyo / Integra / Pioneer A/V receiver over the network (eISCP, the Integra Serial Control Protocol over Ethernet). Power, mute, master volume, input selection, and listening-mode (DSP) selection. Add it by IP address, or let device discovery find it on the network.
help.setup:
1. Connect the receiver to the same network as OpenAVC (Ethernet preferred). 2. In the receiver's network / hardware setup, enable network standby /
   network control (some models only accept eISCP when this is on, and it
   also lets you power the unit on from standby over the network).
3. Add the device and enter its IP address (port 60128 is the eISCP
   default), or run a discovery scan and pick it from the results.
help.connection: eISCP is a bidirectional protocol: the receiver echoes its state after every command and answers the xxxQSTN queries, so power, mute, input, listening mode, and the (hex) master-volume level poll back automatically. If the unit won't respond, confirm network standby / network control is enabled in its setup menu.

compatible_models.notes: Networked Onkyo A/V receivers with eISCP control enabled (Ethernet / Wi-Fi). Same ISCP command set (PWR / AMT / MVL / SLI / LMD) as the RS-232 flavor, wrapped in the eISCP packet header.
Integra (Onkyo's professional line) networked receivers share the same eISCP command set.

Onkyo absorbed Pioneer's A/V receiver line; current Pioneer network receivers speak the same eISCP command set on TCP 60128. Discovery uses the Onkyo "!x" device-search broadcast; Pioneer units also answer a "!p" broadcast, so a Pioneer that stays silent to discovery can still be added by IP address.

drivers.name: Onkyo / Integra AV Receiver (ISCP Serial)
drivers.author: OpenAVC
drivers.description: Controls Onkyo and Integra A/V receivers over RS-232 using the Integra Serial Control Protocol (ISCP). Power, mute, master volume, input selection, and listening-mode (DSP) selection, with polled power / mute / input / listening mode / volume status. A constant "!1" packet header and CR terminator are declared once and wrap every command.

help.overview: Onkyo / Integra A/V receiver over RS-232 (the Integra Serial Control Protocol). Power, mute, master volume, input selection, and listening-mode (DSP) selection. Works on a direct serial port or through an IP-to-serial bridge (choose "Through a bridge" in Connection settings and pick the bridge's RS-232 port).
help.setup:
1. Connect the receiver's RS-232 port (or wire it to a serial bridge). 2. Serial settings are 9600 baud, 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit, no
   flow control. Confirm the baud rate in the receiver's setup menu.
3. In the receiver's setup, make sure serial / RS-232 control is enabled. 4. Add the device and pick its serial port (or the bridge's RS-232 port).
help.connection: ISCP is a bidirectional protocol: the receiver echoes its state after every command and answers the xxxQSTN queries, so power, mute, input, listening mode, and the (hex) master-volume level poll back automatically.

compatible_models.notes: Onkyo A/V receivers with an RS-232 control port using the ISCP command set (PWR / AMT / MVL / SLI / LMD). Verify the serial baud rate in the receiver's setup menu (9600 is the default).
Integra (Onkyo's professional line) receivers share the same ISCP command set over RS-232.

drivers.name: QSC Q-SYS QRC
drivers.author: OpenAVC
drivers.description: Controls QSC Q-SYS Cores via QRC (Q-SYS Remote Control) — JSON-RPC 2.0 over TCP port 1710. Auto-discovers the running design's Components and their controls on connect (no manual block list), models each Component as a typed child entity, and streams real-time state via Change Group auto-poll. Covers Component control, Named Controls, Mixer, Audio Router, Snapshot recall/save, Loop Player, and PA Router paging.

help.overview: Comprehensive QSC Q-SYS control over QRC (JSON-RPC 2.0 on TCP 1710). On connect the driver reads the running design's Components and their controls straight from the Core and lists each Component as a child entity under the device — no block list to type. Every control is subscribed via a Change Group with auto-poll, so bindings update in real time. Use the per-component commands (Set Gain, Set Mute, Mixer …, Recall Snapshot, …) in macros and panels, and 'Re-import Topology' after you change the Q-SYS design.
help.setup:
STEP 1 — Expose your blocks in Q-SYS Designer.
For each block you want to control (Gain, Mixer, Router, Snapshot Controller, Loop Player, …), open its Properties and set 'Script Access' to 'External' (or 'All'). Give it a clear 'Code Name'. Components WITHOUT Script Access = External are invisible to QRC — this is the #1 setup mistake. Save to Core & Run (F5) so the change takes effect.

STEP 2 — (Optional) Named Controls.
Individual controls you drag into Designer's Named Controls list (e.g. 'Volume', 'Mute') can be monitored too. QRC cannot enumerate these, so add each one you want to the 'Named Controls' table on the device page (Name, plus an optional type — number/boolean/string/trigger). Most rooms need none, since Components are discovered automatically.

STEP 3 — Enter the Core's IP address above.
If the Core has authentication enabled (Core Manager → Users), fill in Username and Password; otherwise leave them blank.

STEP 4 — Save. Within a second or two the device connects, the Core's status (Active/Idle/Standby), model, design name, and health populate, and each exposed Component appears under the device's Components tab with its live, typed controls. Bind child state (e.g. device.<id>.component.PgmGain.gain) to UI elements, or drive commands like 'Set Gain' / 'Recall Snapshot' from macros and panel buttons.

Troubleshooting:
  • No components listed — the blocks aren't exposed. Set Script Access = External in Designer and redeploy (F5). Use the 'Test Connection' action to list what QRC currently sees.
  • 'Connection refused' on 1710 — the Core isn't in Run mode, or a VLAN ACL blocks QRC.
  • Logon errors — set Username/Password to match a Q-SYS user.
  • Design changed — run the 'Re-import Topology' action (or the Components tab's Refresh) to re-read the control surface.
  • Need something the typed commands don't cover — use 'Set Component Control' or 'Send Raw JSON-RPC'.

compatible_models.notes: Verified end-to-end against a live Core 24f: auto-discovery (Component.GetComponents / GetControls), change-group push, and round-trips for gain/mute, mixer crosspoint, router, snapshot, and Named Controls.

Every Q-SYS Core that runs Q-SYS Designer speaks QRC (TCP 1710) — the same protocol verified on the Core 24f — so these are expected to work but haven't been tested on real hardware. This driver uses QRC, not the legacy ECP (TCP 1702). In Designer, set each block's Script Access to External (or All) so it appears in auto-discovery; add Named Controls to the Named Controls list to monitor them.

drivers.name: Shure Networked Devices
drivers.author: OpenAVC
drivers.description: Controls Shure networked audio devices over the Device Control Strings protocol on TCP port 2202 — MXA910 / MXA920 / MXA710 ceiling arrays, ANI interfaces, the P300 IntelliMix processor, and the SCM820 automixer. Each audio channel is a child entity with mute, gain, name, and live metering; device-level mute, presets, and status LED are controlled directly. Channel state pushes live as it changes on the device or another controller.

help.overview:
Shure networked microphones, interfaces, and processors speak the Device Control Strings (DCS) protocol on TCP port 2202. This driver models each audio channel as a child entity carrying its mute, gain (in dB), name, and live level, and controls device-level mute, presets, and the status LED directly.

State is push-driven: after connecting, the driver seeds every channel from the device, then mirrors the REP messages the device sends whenever anything changes — including changes made on the front panel or in Shure Designer.

Channel names are read-only over third-party control — set them in Shure Designer, and they appear here as the channel labels.
help.setup:
1. In Shure Designer (or the device web UI), the third-party control interface on TCP 2202 is enabled by default.
2. Give the device a static IP or a DHCP reservation.
3. In OpenAVC, enter the IP. Port 2202 is fixed.
4. Set Channel Count to match the device (e.g. 9 for an MXA array's 8 lobes plus the automixer output, 4 for an ANI4IN). Over-sizing is harmless — extra channels just answer REP ERR — but clutters the channel list.
5. To see live level meters, set Meter Interval to a value like 500 ms (0 disables metering).

compatible_models.notes: All speak the same Device Control Strings grammar. Channel counts differ by model — set Channel Count to match: MXA arrays have 8 mic channels plus the automixer output (9), the ANI4IN/4OUT have 4, the SCM820 has 8 inputs plus mixes, and the P300 has a large input/output matrix. Device mute and presets are MXA / P300 / ANI; the SCM820 mutes per channel and has no presets — unsupported properties answer a benign REP ERR.

drivers.name: Sonos Speaker
drivers.author: OpenAVC
drivers.description: Controls Sonos speakers via the local UPnP API. Play/pause, volume, mute, bass/treble, track info, and transport control. The speaker pushes state changes as they happen (UPnP eventing).

help.overview: Controls any Sonos speaker on the local network via UPnP. Works with all Sonos models including One, Five, Beam, Arc, Era, Move, Roam, Port, Amp, and legacy Play/Connect models. No cloud account or API key required. The speaker pushes state changes as they happen, so transport state, volume, mute and now-playing info update on panels within about a second — whether the change came from OpenAVC, the Sonos app, or a button on the speaker itself.
help.setup:
1. Ensure the Sonos speaker is on the same network
2. Enter the speaker's IP address (find it in the Sonos app under Settings > System > About)
3. Default port is 1400 (do not change)
4. UPnP control must be enabled on the speaker (on by default)
5. For instant updates the speaker must be able to reach the OpenAVC server, because it posts events back to it. If a firewall sits between them, allow that direction too. Without it everything still works, just at poll speed.

compatible_models.notes: UPnP API stable across all Sonos models. Control and eventing verified on a Sonos Amp (S16) and a Sonos One (S18), firmware 95.1 (S2).

drivers.name: Symetrix Composer DSP
drivers.author: OpenAVC
drivers.description: Controls Symetrix Edge, Radius, Radius AEC, Radius NX, Prism, Solus NX, and xControl DSPs via the Composer Control Protocol on TCP port 48631. Generic controller model: assign controller numbers (1–10000) in Composer to faders, mutes, selectors, and meters; this driver reads / writes those numbers and subscribes to push-enabled value changes.

help.overview: Symetrix DSPs use a generic external-control model: the AV integrator wires controller numbers to specific DSP elements in Composer (Tools → Controller Manager) with the 'Enable Push' setting active. This driver speaks that protocol, so macros can move controllers, recall presets, and react to DSP state changes without writing custom protocol code.
help.setup:
1. In Composer, open Tools → Controller Manager and assign controller numbers (1–10000) to the faders, mutes, selectors, and meters you want to control from OpenAVC. Make sure the 'Push' checkbox is enabled for each.
2. Compile and push the design to the unit.
3. Note the unit's IP address (System Manager).
4. Enter the IP, port 48631, and num_controllers (set to the highest controller number you assigned, rounded up — default 64 covers most installations) in the device config in OpenAVC.
5. Connect. The driver enables global push and issues Push Refresh on connect, so all current values populate immediately.

compatible_models.notes: Every Symetrix DSP that runs Composer 3.0+ shares the same Control Protocol on TCP 48631. Newer NX models require Composer 6.0+. The driver's controller-number coverage is bounded only by the configured num_controllers value (default 64, max 256).

drivers.name: TOA 9000M2 Matrix Mixer
drivers.author: OpenAVC
drivers.description: Controls the TOA M-9000M2 Digital Matrix Mixer and protocol-compatible A-9000M2 Series mixer/amplifiers over RS-232C. 8 mixing inputs x 8 outputs: input/output fader gain, the 8x8 crosspoint matrix, channel on/off, tone, parametric EQ, loudness, HPF/LPF, input sensitivity, phantom power, preset / paging-event recall, speaker presets, and ANC. The device is write-then-echo with no live readback except channel names and ANC reference, so state is tracked optimistically from the confirmations it returns.

help.overview:
The TOA 9000M2 Series speaks a compact binary RS-232C protocol: every message is <command byte> <length> <data...>. This driver exposes the full control surface for the 8x8 matrix mixer -- faders, the crosspoint matrix, mutes, tone, parametric EQ, filters, loudness, input sensitivity, phantom power, presets, paging events, speaker presets, and ANC.

IMPORTANT -- feedback is limited. The hardware confirms each command by echoing it back, so the driver knows a change was accepted and mirrors it in state. But the protocol has NO way to read most current values back; the only true reads are channel names and the ANC reference level. As a result, changes made at the unit's front panel or by a scene recall will not appear in OpenAVC. Drive the mixer entirely from OpenAVC (or re-send known values on connect) for state to stay accurate. Fader 'nudge' commands are the exception -- the device returns the resulting level, which is read back exactly.
help.setup:
1. Wire RS-232C to the unit's D-sub 9-pin port with a STRAIGHT cable (pin 2 = TX, pin 3 = RX, pin 5 = GND).
2. Set the serial port path in the device config (e.g. COM3 on Windows, /dev/ttyUSB0 on Linux) and pick the baud rate that matches the unit (9600 / 19200 / 38400 / 57600; 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit).
3. To route the mixer over the network, connect it to an IP-to-serial bridge (e.g. Global Cache iTach) and bind this device to the bridge's serial port -- OpenAVC carries the bytes through transparently.

Commands cannot be received while the unit is powered off (send Power On first).

compatible_models.notes: Digital Matrix Mixer. 8 mic/line inputs x 8 outputs. RS-232C, D-sub 9-pin, 9600-57600 8N1, straight cable.
9000M2 Series mixer/amplifiers share this RS-232C protocol. Power, phantom, and speaker-preset commands are most relevant to these amp models.

drivers.name: Turtle AV Dante Bluetooth Wallplate
drivers.author: OpenAVC
drivers.description: Controls the Turtle AV Dante Bluetooth Wallplate (WPD20BUS) over Telnet. Bridges a stereo Bluetooth source into Dante. Input gain/mute/stereo, Bluetooth pairing window, volume, mute, audio bridging mode, transport (play/pause/skip) with now-playing metadata, connection status, and per-channel parametric EQ.

help.overview: Controls the Turtle AV Dante Bluetooth Wallplate. The wall plate streams two channels of Bluetooth audio into a Dante network. Use this driver to manage input gain and mute, the Bluetooth pairing window, playback volume and transport, audio bridging mode, and per-channel EQ. Audio routing, sample rate, and Dante latency are configured in Dante Controller.
help.setup:
1. Connect the wall plate's DANTE (PoE) port to your network switch and
   power it (PoE or 12 V DC).
2. Find the device's IP address in Dante Controller (Device Info tab). 3. Enter that IP address here. The control port defaults to 23 (Telnet).
   If you moved control to the raw TCP/IP port, set the port to 8000.
4. Pair a phone or laptop: press "Pairing On" (or the front-panel button)
   and select the wall plate in the source device's Bluetooth settings.
5. The wall plate has no control-channel password — credentials in the
   Dante Web GUI protect that web interface only.

compatible_models.notes: Dante Bluetooth Wallplate, 2x2 (US). The device model is confirmed at connect via "get type" (answers WPD20BUS).

drivers.name: Yamaha MTX/MRX/XMV
drivers.author: OpenAVC
drivers.description: Controls Yamaha install-audio processors (MTX3, MTX5-D, MRX7-D) and the XMV power amps + EXi8 / EXo8 audio expanders over the Remote Control Protocol (RCP) on TCP port 49280. Push-capable: NOTIFY messages from the device drive state immediately; polling backstops refresh and a liveness watchdog detects a silently dead link. MRX7-D parameters are addressed via Remote Control Setup List Index numbers (1..32); MTX/XMV use full parameter paths via generic set_param / get_param.

help.overview:
Yamaha RCP is the unified ASCII control protocol used across the MTX, MRX, XMV, EXi8, and EXo8 product family. The protocol is push-capable - the device sends a NOTIFY message whenever a parameter changes, whether from this controller, the front panel, another remote controller, or a preset/snapshot recall.
For MRX7-D, integrators define a Remote Control Setup List in MTX-MRX Editor that maps each panel control (fader, mute, selector) to an Index number. This driver exposes 32 Index slots; bind your panel UI to the set_index / inc_index / query_index commands.
For MTX3 / MTX5-D / XMV / EXi8 / EXo8, addresses look like MTX:mem_512/60000/0/0/0/0/0 - the seven-element path identifies a specific channel/parameter. Look up addresses in section 7 ("Parameter List") of the RCP specification, then use set_param / get_param / inc_param.
help.setup:
1. Connect the Yamaha device(s) to the network via Ethernet. 2. In MTX-MRX Editor (or ProVisionaire Edit for newer firmware), open
   System -> Remote Control. Enable network remote control on TCP port
   49280. The device supports up to 8 simultaneous remote sessions.
3. (MRX7-D only) In MTX-MRX Editor, open Remote Control Setup List.
   Assign each panel control to an Index number 1..32. Synchronize the
   project to the device.
4. Enter the device's IP address in the OpenAVC device config. Leave
   port at 49280.
5. Optional: set keepalive_timeout > 0 to enable RCP keepalive for
   unreliable networks. The device will drop the connection if no
   command arrives within the configured timeout.

compatible_models.notes: Matrix processors. MRX7-D requires a Remote Control Setup List in MTX-MRX Editor that maps user faders / mutes / selectors to Index numbers; this driver controls them by Index. MTX3 / MTX5-D use full parameter addresses via the generic set_param command.
XMV power amps. Controlled via full parameter paths (set_param / get_param). RCP control is independent of any MTX/MRX in the system.
Audio I/O expanders. Same RCP address model as XMV.
